page9_img_1.png.title: Productivity Pressure Paradox cycle linking expectations to unrealized AI gains
page9_img_1.png.description: A four-step feedback loop of purple boxes connected by arrows: “Increased Productivity Expectations (Pressure for Immediate Gains)” points to “Tighter Deadlines (No Time To Learn)”, which points to “Revert to Familiar Methods (Minimal Tool Use)”, which leads to “Limited Productivity Gains (Unrealized ROI)”, and loops back to heightened expectations. The diagram emphasizes that managerial expectations for rapid AI-driven productivity create time pressure that prevents the experimentation and learning needed to integrate GenAI, producing the very limited gains organizations hoped for. A gold box at the bottom—“Breaking the Cycle: Context-Specific Resources + Time”—is shown as the intervention to interrupt the loop by providing targeted guidance and protected learning time. This visual summarizes the paper’s argument that organizational pressure without scaffolding produces a self-perpetuating barrier to realizing GenAI benefits.

page4_img_figure_1.png.title: Density plot of GenAI usage days for frequent vs. infrequent users
page4_img_figure_1.png.description: A kernel density plot showing the distribution of days each group used a GenAI development tool over an 8‑week (56‑day) window. The gold (infrequent) curve is tightly concentrated near the left of the axis with a peak around ~5–10 days, reflecting the paper’s reported median of 5.5 days; the purple (frequent) curve peaks near ~30–35 days (reported median 33 days) with a smaller shoulder toward ~40+ days. The two smoothed distributions are largely separated with only a small overlap around ~18–22 days, visually substantiating the paper’s distinction between team‑matched frequent and infrequent users.

page4_img_1.png.title: GenAI tool usage density: frequent vs. infrequent users
page4_img_1.png.description: A kernel density plot comparing days of GenAI (GitHub Copilot) use over an eight‑week (56 day) window for two groups: “Infrequent” (gold) and “Frequent” (purple). The x‑axis shows number of days used (0–56) and the y‑axis shows user density; the infrequent group has a sharp peak at very low use (around ~3–8 days, consistent with the paper’s median of 5.5 days) while the frequent group peaks near ~30–35 days (paper median 33 days) with a smaller secondary bump near ~40 days. The two shaded distributions are largely separated with only modest overlap around ~20 days, illustrating a clear distinction between low and high users that the study used to form matched pairs within teams.

page5_img_1.png.title: Traits distinguishing frequent and infrequent GenAI tool users
page5_img_1.png.description: A paired horizontal bar visualization that contrasts attributes linked to frequent (purple) and infrequent (gold) GenAI development tool users across eight factors. For each factor the chart shows which group more commonly exhibited the attribute: frequent users are dominant for ‘Collaborator,’ ‘Realistic’ expectations, ‘Experimental’ adoption, ‘Continuous’ integration, ‘Self‑Directed’ learning, ‘Adaptive Persistence,’ ‘Confident Adaptation,’ and ‘AI‑Fluency’; infrequent users are dominant for the opposing attributes (‘Feature,’ ‘Misaligned’ expectations, ‘Conservative,’ ‘Task‑Specific,’ ‘Minimal/Constrained’ learning, ‘Quick Abandonment,’ ‘AI Replacement Anxiety,’ and ‘Skill Continuity’). The legend (purple = Frequent Users, gold = Infrequent Users) and relative bar lengths indicate the strength of association reported in the interviews and summarize the paper’s core finding that these paired, contrasting mindsets and behaviors distinguish frequent from infrequent adopters within shared team contexts.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Participant demographics: location, role, and Copilot experience (N=54)
page4_img_table_1.png.description: Table 1 summarizes the study sample (N=54). Participants were predominately U.S.-based (36, 66.7%) with smaller numbers in China (6, 11.1%), Kenya (4, 7.4%) and several other countries (each 2, 3.7%). Most respondents were senior software engineers (32, 59.3%), followed by mid-level SWE II (18, 33.3%) and a few junior-level SWEs (4, 7.4%). Reported GitHub Copilot experience skews toward longer use: 21 participants (38.9%) had 1–2 years, 13 (24.1%) had 2–3 years, while 11 (20.4%) had <6 months and 9 (16.7%) had 6–12 months of use.

page11_img_1.png.title: Evidence-based Team Interventions for GenAI Adoption
page11_img_1.png.description: A four-column table summarizing six team-level interventions (left column) mapped to the adoption stage they target, the mechanism by which they work, and concrete implementation examples. Interventions are: Clear Organizational Messaging (targets mindset formation; e.g., leadership demos, documented value propositions, success metrics), AI Tool Champions (approach determination; e.g., 1–2 designated team experts with ~10% time for peer support), Context-Specific Use Cases and Knowledge Sharing Infrastructure (experience & learning; e.g., team wiki with repository examples, dedicated chat channel, ‘AI wins/fails’ in standups, pair programming), Protected Learning Time (throughout; e.g., “AI Fridays”, sprint time allocation, hackathons), and Collaborative Sessions (experience & learning; e.g., weekly demos, monthly challenges, brown-bag talks). These entries align with the paper’s findings that teams need concrete, context-specific scaffolding, social learning structures, and sanctioned time to overcome the Productivity Pressure Paradox and enable effective GenAI tool integration.

page11_img_table_1.png.title: Team interventions to support GenAI adoption
page11_img_table_1.png.description: Table 2 enumerates six evidence-based team interventions (Clear Organizational Messaging; AI Tool Champions; Context-Specific Use Cases; Knowledge Sharing Infrastructure; Protected Learning Time; Collaborative Sessions) across four columns: Intervention, Target Stage, Mechanism, and Implementation Examples. Each row maps a concrete organizational action to the stage of adoption it targets and the mechanism by which it helps (for example, Clear Organizational Messaging targets mindset formation by setting expectations and legitimizing exploration, with implementation examples like leadership demos and documented value propositions). Other rows show pragmatic practices: AI Tool Champions (1–2 designated experts with ~10% time) model usage and reduce risk; Context-Specific Use Cases translate capabilities to team workflows via a team wiki with domain examples; Knowledge Sharing Infrastructure accelerates learning and normalizes failures (dedicated channels, ‘AI wins/fails’ in standups); Protected Learning Time enables pressure-free experimentation (AI Fridays, sprint allocation, hackathons); and Collaborative Sessions convert individual struggles into team learning (weekly demos, monthly challenges, brown-bag talks). Overall the table links specific interventions to mechanisms intended to lower individual learning burden and address the productivity-pressure challenges discussed in the paper.

page1_img_1.png.title: Framework of individual and organizational drivers of developer GenAI adoption
page1_img_1.png.description: A staged flow diagram linking four adoption stages—(1) Mindset Formation, (2) Approach Determination, (3) Experience & Learning, and (4) Integration & Evolution—where each stage shows paired individual-factor polarities in purple ovals (e.g., Tool Perception: collaborator vs. feature; Performance Expectations: realistic vs. misaligned; Adoption Approach: experimental vs. conservative; Integration Strategy: continuous vs. task-specific; Learning Strategy: self-directed vs. constrained; Response to Failure: adaptive persistence vs. quick abandonment; Role Evolution and Skill Evolution). A gray box between stages labels “Initial Trials” and “Encounters w/ Challenges/Failures,” indicating early setbacks as a hinge point that shapes subsequent learning and responses. Gold arrows on the right label external supports—AI Champions, Exploration Time, Context‑Specific Resources, Knowledge Sharing Structures, and Clear Messaging—that the paper identifies as team/organizational levers that can shift individuals toward exploratory, persistent learning and eventual AI‑fluency rather than constrained, abandonment-prone behavior. The figure summarizes the paper’s claim that individual perceptions and behaviors interact dynamically with these external factors to determine long‑term integration of GenAI in development work.
